newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai exchange rivals Tocom for Asia dominance.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai exchange rivals Tocom for Asia dominance.

text.p: The Shanghai Metal Exchange could become Asia's premier metals trading floor as its major rival, the Tokyo Commodities Exchange, is not being widely used by the international metals trade, industry sources said.
Western metals industry executives said on Thursday the Tokyo Commodities Exchange, TOCOM, was not providing a favourable environment for traders who use the London Metal Exchange (LME).

TOCOM was established in 1984 with the merger of Tokyo's gold, rubber and textile commodities exchanges. It launched trading in its yen-based aluminium futures contract in early April, the first base metals futures contract ever traded in Japan.
Initial volumes have been smaller than the 20,000 lots per day originally expected, but the exchange has said liquidity will grow as new contracts are listed later this year.
Japanese metals industry leaders have said, however, that they see no need to list a copper futures contract on TOCOM.
"The structure of TOCOM is not favourable to traders who use the LME," said Michael Hutchinson, managing director of Metallgesellschaft Ltd.
Volumes were small, he said, and contract size was geared to small investors instead of being driven by producers and users of aluminium.
"For the foreseeable future we don't think TOCOM will add very much to aluminium trading in the world," he said.
The TOCOM aluminium contract had been seen as the first step toward a fully-fledged metals trading floor, which another western trader said had been discussed since the early 1970s.

"The Japanese have been considering a metal exchange for copper since 1971, and it still isn't on the drawing board," said David Waite, director of business development for London broker Rudoph Wolff.
He said that while most metals futures business is currently done on the LME because that is where the liquidity is, there is a battle going on for the Pacific time zone.
"In five years time, liquidity can be moved into the Pacific time zone." he said.

"The main rival (to China) is probably Japan, but both Japanese companies and the government have been more cautiously inclined to preserve the internal pricing status quo rather than face the international challenge," he said.
"I think Chinese trading skills and Chinese trading instincts, combined with the attitude of their authorities, are likely to be more aggressive than those of the Japanese," he said.

"We haven't seen that the Chinese government is willing to be more expansive yet, but judging by the way the Chinese look at trading issues generally, one has to assume they will find a way to work it out," Waite said.
"The prize is a big one and the SHME (Shanghai Metal Exchange) is in as good a position as any to grasp it," he said.
Which of China's 14 commodities exchanges would be the eventual survivor and become Asia's premier remained to be seen, he said.
The Shanghai exchange was strong in copper, but traded only a few hundred tonnes of aluminium a day.
"Clearly having one centre for liquidity is the way to go," he said.

Hutchinson, Waite and some other Western industry representatives were in Shanghai at the invitation of the Shanghai Metal Exchange which is celebrating its fifth anniversary. --Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
